items.title: Home
items.text:
Survives restarts. The state travels inside the message. Add Redis or Postgres when it outgrows the message or many people click at once.

Components V2 first. Build with containers, sections and galleries. A row of buttons is the simple case.

Typed all the way. risa passes pyright strict, so your editor knows every field.

Coming from miru? See what changes.

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Click it. In a real bot the count survives a restart, because it lives in the button itself.

items.title: API reference
items.text:
A component handler for hikari, built on Discord's Components V2.

A view is a class whose fields are its state, whose render returns its layout, and whose handlers answer the clicks on it. The state travels inside the message by default, so views survive restarts with no infrastructure. A view that outgrows the message can keep its state in a store.

items.title: Client
items.text:
Client(
    rest: RESTClient,
    *,
    use_global: bool = False,
    di: DependencyInjectionManager | None = None,
    register_app_dependencies: bool = True,
    auto_defer: AutoDefer = OFF,
    auto_defer_delay: float = AUTO_DEFER_DELAY,
    store: Store | None = None,
    stores: Mapping[str, Store] | None = None,
    key_prefix: str | None = None,
)

Bases: ABC

Routes clicks on registered views to their handlers.

Make one with client_from_app or client_from_lightbulb, add views with add_view, and send a view with build. A client answers only custom_ids risa wrote, so it can share a bot with other component handlers.

Parameters:

  • rest (RESTClient) –

    The REST client risa answers interactions through.

  • use_global (bool, default: False ) –

    Also route views registered with @risa.register but never added to this client.

  • di (DependencyInjectionManager | None, default: None ) –

    The linkd manager handlers are injected from; a new one by default.

  • register_app_dependencies (bool, default: True ) –

    Register the app, its REST client, and its event manager or interaction server for injection.

  • auto_defer (AutoDefer, default: OFF ) –

    The AutoDefer of views and handlers that set none, OFF by default.

  • auto_defer_delay (float, default: AUTO_DEFER_DELAY ) –

  • store (Store | None, default: None ) –

    The store InStore views use unless they name another.

  • stores (Mapping[str, Store] | None, default: None ) –

  • key_prefix (str | None, default: None ) –

items.text:
build(view: View) -> Rendered

Render view into the components of a new message, ready to send.

await ctx.respond(**await client.build(Poll(question="Ship it?")))

It runs the view's load, renders it, and writes an InStore view's first record. The result spreads into any hikari or lightbulb call that takes components=. If that send fails, the record stays behind until its TTL reaps it, or for good under InStore(ttl=None).

    If the view's class was never registered.

  • ViewDeclarationError –

    If the view keeps its state in a store this client does not have.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state does not fit its components.

How InMessage state is written into custom_id characters.

BASE85, the default, is built in and keeps every character printable ASCII. BASE32768 and URO14 come with the [radixly] extra and carry more than twice as many bytes per character.

items.title: edit async
items.text:
edit(layout: Layout) -> None

Replace the message with layout, keeping the view's state on it.

For a screen the view's render does not draw, such as a confirmation or a closing message. A layout without interactive components ends the view, since nothing on it can be clicked any more. Like rerender(), it saves the view's state.

Parameters:

  • layout (Layout) –

    The new layout: one top-level component, or several in order.

Raises:

  • NoViewError –

    If the layout has interactive components and the view has durable fields, but this context has no view state, as in on_outdated and on_state_missing.

  • EphemeralOriginError –

    If the message is ephemeral and the interaction was answered with a new message.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state does not fit the layout's components.

  • StateConflictError –

    If another process saved the view's state first. The view then holds that state.

items.title: rerender async
items.text:
rerender() -> None

Redraw the message from the view's current state, and save that state.

Every rerender is a commit. InMessage state is written into the message itself; InStore state goes to the store first, then the message is edited. A change made without calling it is saved when the handler returns, but that save can only log a failure; call it yourself, before any respond(), where a failure must be handled.

Raises:

  • NoViewError –

    If the view has durable fields but this context has no view state, as in on_outdated and on_state_missing.

  • EphemeralOriginError –

    If the message is ephemeral and the interaction was answered with a new message.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state no longer fits its components.

  • StateConflictError –

    If another process saved the view's state first. The view then holds that state, and the handler can apply its change again and rerender.

  • StateNotFoundError –

    If an InStore view's record disappeared while the handler ran.

items.title: AutoDefer
items.text:
Bases: StrEnum

How risa answers a click whose handler has not answered in time.

Discord fails an interaction that gets no answer within three seconds. With auto-defer, risa acknowledges the click in the handler's place after the client's auto_defer_delay, and the handler carries on. Set it on the client, on a view with @risa.register(defer=...), or on a handler with @risa.handler(defer=...); the most specific setting wins.

Attributes:

  • OFF –

    Never answer in the handler's place. The default.

  • UPDATE –

    Acknowledge silently, for a handler that answers with ctx.rerender() or ctx.edit(...).

  • THINKING –

    Show a "thinking..." message, for a handler that answers with ctx.respond(...), which then takes its place.

  • THINKING_EPHEMERAL –

    The same, visible only to the user who clicked.

items.title: View
items.text:
Bases: Struct

Base class of a view: a message's layout, its state, and the handlers behind it.

A view is a msgspec.Struct, and its annotated fields are its durable state, carried from click to click. Mark a field risa.Prop[...] to rebuild it fresh on every click instead, typically in load. Register the class with @risa.register, return its layout from render, and send it with client.build:

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Row(ui.Button(self.add, label=f"Clicks: {self.count}"))

    @risa.handler
    async def add(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Each click runs its handler on the latest saved state of its view, and clicks on one view queue up within a process, each waiting up to ten seconds for the lock; one that waits longer is logged and goes unanswered. A view without durable fields has nothing to protect and takes no lock, so its handlers may run at the same time. Across processes, an InStore view on a shared store lets the first write win, while for an InMessage view the last edit of the message wins. A change made without ctx.rerender() is saved when the handler returns, but that save can only log a failure, so a handler that must know calls ctx.rerender() itself, before any ctx.respond(). A handler that raises keeps what it saved through rerender() or edit() before, and loses the rest.

on_outdated(ctx: ComponentContext) -> None

Answer a click on a component this view can no longer route.

The component's handler was retired by a version bump, its wire parameters changed without one, or its state was written by durable fields the view no longer has. The default does nothing, so the click fails on the user's side, and risa logs it. Override it to answer the user, or to replace the dead message with ctx.edit(...). Its parameters are injected, as a handler's are, and ctx has no view state.

To answer clicks on one retired handler differently, keep a method with its id, version and wire parameters whose body says the component is outdated. It routes like any handler, and nothing is logged.

Parameters:

  • ctx (ComponentContext) –

    The context of the click, which has no view state.

items.title: handler
items.text:
handler(func: HandlerFunction[V, P]) -> HandlerMethod[V, P]

handler(
    *,
    handler_id: str | None = ...,
    version: int = ...,
    defer: AutoDefer | None = ...,
) -> _HandlerDecorator

Make a view method a handler that components can route to.

Used bare it returns the handler, and with options a decorator that makes one. A handler takes the view and a ComponentContext, then its wire parameters, then anything to inject:

@risa.handler(defer=risa.AutoDefer.UPDATE)
async def vote(
    self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, option: int, db: Database
) -> None: ...

Wire parameters come first, are positional, and are annotated bool, int, str, hikari.Snowflake or an enum.Enum of int or str values. They receive the values risa.bind put on the component. Every parameter after them without a default is injected through linkd, so a hikari enum such as hikari.ChannelType, which is not an enum.Enum, is injected too; to carry one on the wire, bind its value as an int. To inject an int or another of those types, default it to risa.di.INJECTED. A handler returns None.

Parameters:

  • func (Callable[..., Awaitable[None]] | None, default: None ) –

    The view method to make a handler. Left out, the call takes options and returns the decorator.

  • handler_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    The id the handler routes under, the method's name by default. Pin it before renaming the method, so components already sent keep working.

  • version (int, default: 1 ) –

    Bump it when the wire parameters change. Components sent before keep routing to a method that still has the old version; once none does, they go to View.on_outdated.

  • defer (AutoDefer | None, default: None ) –

    The handler's AutoDefer, overriding the view's.

items.title: InMessage
items.text:
InMessage(codec: Codec = BASE85)

Bases: Struct

Keep a view's durable state inside the message it renders.

The default placement. The state is written into the spare characters of the rendered components' custom_ids and read back from the message on every click. It needs no infrastructure, survives restarts, and lives exactly as long as the message. It is bounded by what the components can carry: up to about 70 bytes per interactive component with the default codec.

The state is readable by anyone who can see the message, so never keep secrets in durable fields. A click cannot change it: risa reads it from the message Discord delivers with the click.

A rerender that changes the state changes the custom_id of the buttons that carry it. In tests Discord refused a click on a custom_id the message no longer has, so someone whose client still shows the old button gets a failed click and can click again. Discord does not document this and risa does not check it, so do not rely on the refusal. A view many people click at once fits InStore better: its custom_ids hold a key instead of the state, so they change only when a bound argument does.

Attributes:

  • codec (Codec) –

    How the state is written into custom_ids. risa.codecs.BASE85 by default; BASE32768 and URO14 from the [radixly] extra carry more than twice as much.

InStore(ttl: float | None, store: str = DEFAULT_STORE)

Keep a view's durable state in a store, under a key the message carries.

The components carry only a random key, and the state is one record in the client's store of the name store. It has no size bound, every process of a bot shares it through a distributed store, and it expires.

    Seconds an untouched record lives. Every click restarts the clock, so only abandoned views expire. None keeps records forever, including the ones a deleted message or a failed send leaves behind. There is no default, since no lifetime suits both a confirmation dialog and a role menu.

  • store (str) –

    Which of the client's stores holds the state: "default" for the client's store=, or a key of its stores=.

items.text:
PostgresStore(
    pool: Pool,
    *,
    table: str = DEFAULT_TABLE,
    lease: float = DEFAULT_LEASE,
    max_hold: float = DEFAULT_MAX_HOLD,
)

Bases: Store

A store on PostgreSQL, through an asyncpg pool.

An entry is a row of table. lock() takes a lease on a row of {table}_lease and renews it while held, so clicks on one view queue up across every process that shares the database. The store creates both tables on first use if they are missing, and deletes expired rows itself: on its first write, then on every hundredth.

Parameters:

    The pool the bot owns. The store borrows a connection for each statement and never opens or closes the pool.

  • table (str, default: DEFAULT_TABLE ) –

    The name of the state table: a lowercase identifier of at most 52 characters. The lease table is named after it.

  • lease (float, default: DEFAULT_LEASE ) –

    Seconds a lock's lease lasts. It is renewed every third of that while held, and a crashed holder blocks its view for at most this long.

  • max_hold (float, default: DEFAULT_MAX_HOLD ) –

    Seconds after which a held lock is no longer renewed, so a stuck handler cannot block its view for good.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If table is not a plain lowercase identifier, lease is not positive, or max_hold is shorter than lease.

items.title: Coming from miru
items.text:
hikari-risa is not a direct successor to miru, so it does some things differently. Much of it will still look familiar: a view class, methods that answer clicks, a client that routes them. The big change is where a view lives. A miru view is an object in your bot's memory. A risa view is rebuilt on every click, from state kept in the message or in a store you choose.

This page compares with miru 4.3.1. The main things miru has and risa does not are under What risa does not have. risa needs Python 3.12 to 3.15, and miru 4.3.1 needs 3.11 or newer.

items.title: The same things under other names
items.text: miru risa class MyView(miru.View) @risa.register(name="my-view") above class MyView(risa.View) self.x = 0 in __init__ An annotated field, x: int = 0 @miru.button(...) on a callback (self, ctx, button) @risa.handler on a method (self, ctx), and ui.Button(self.method, ...) in render() @miru.text_select(...) and select.values ui.TextSelect(self.method, ...) and ctx.values miru.Button subclasses that hold a value One handler with an argument, ui.Button(risa.bind(self.method, value)) view.add_item(...) and remove_item(...) if and for in render() miru.ViewContext risa.ComponentContext ctx.view self await ctx.edit_response(components=self) await ctx.rerender() ctx.respond("Hi", flags=hikari.MessageFlag.EPHEMERAL) ctx.respond("Hi", ephemeral=True) miru.Client(bot) risa.client_from_app(bot), or risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client) with lightbulb client.start_view(view) after each send client.add_view(MyView) once at startup respond("Hi", components=view) respond(**await client.build(MyView())) timeout=, 120 seconds by default InStore(ttl=...), and no expiry in the message autodefer=True by default, after 2 seconds AutoDefer.OFF by default; set it on a handler, view or client alluka, with @client.inject_dependencies linkd, with no decorator; risa.handler says which parameters are injected

items.title: A view
items.text:
miru's guide to editing items has a counter. This is its counter button:

miru
class EditView(miru.View):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.counter = 0

    @miru.button(label="Counter: 0", style=hikari.ButtonStyle.PRIMARY)
    async def counter_button(
        self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button
    ) -> None:
        self.counter += 1
        button.label = f"Counter: {self.counter}"
        await ctx.edit_response(components=self)

And this is a counter in risa:

risa
@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Three things differ:

  • Items come from render(). A miru item is an object you change. A risa button is drawn again on every rerender, so you change the fields and the button follows.
  • The whole message is the view. A miru 4.3.1 view builds action rows, and you pass content and embeds beside them. A risa view renders with Components V2: containers, sections, galleries and rows. Such a message has no content, so the text goes in ui.TextDisplay.
  • There is no __init__. A view is a msgspec.Struct, made with Counter(count=3), and its annotated fields are saved from click to click. For what should not be saved, such as a database row, mark the field risa.Prop[T] and fill it in load(), which runs before every handler.

items.title: Sending
items.text:
In miru, each message gets its own view object, which you start after sending:

miru
view = EditView()
await event.message.respond("Hello miru!", components=view)
client.start_view(view)

In risa, you add the class once. client.build renders an instance for each message, and nothing needs starting:

risa
client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
client.add_view(Counter)

@bot.listen()
async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
    if event.content == "!counter":
        rendered = await client.build(Counter())
        await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

The result spreads into any call that takes components=, so inside a handler it reads await ctx.respond(**await client.build(Counter())).

items.title: Restarts
items.text:
miru's guide to persistent views says that after a restart "your views will no longer work, even if the timeout did not expire". The answer there is a persistent view: timeout=None, a custom_id on every item, and starting the view again at startup.

miru
class Persistence(miru.View):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(timeout=None)

    @miru.button(label="Button 1", custom_id="my_unique_custom_id_1")
    async def button_one(self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("You pressed button 1.")


@bot.listen()
async def start_views(event: hikari.StartedEvent) -> None:
    client.start_view(Persistence(), bind_to=None)

An unbound view like this one serves every message of its type and does not know which message it is on. A bound view serves one message: you pass its id, which you keep yourself, or it binds to the first message clicked. Either way, you bring back whatever the view held.

In risa, the Counter above already survives a restart. add_view at startup is the whole setup, there is no timeout=None and no custom_id, and each message keeps its own count. See Restart it for how that works.

This has costs:

  • The view's name is its route, and so is its version, which you raise when you change its fields or move it to a store. Either change retires the buttons already sent. Appending a field with a default needs no new version.
  • State in the message has limited room: about 60 bytes on one button, and about 70 more for each further one, with the default codec. Anyone who can see the message can read it.
  • A rerender that changes state in the message changes the id of the button that holds it, and Discord refuses a click on the old id. If two people click at nearly the same moment, the second can fail and click again. A view in a store keeps its ids unless a bound argument changes.
  • A view in a MemoryStore does not survive a restart. Use RedisStore or PostgresStore for that.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text:
A miru view times out after 120 seconds of inactivity unless you pass another timeout=. Then on_timeout() runs and the view stops.

miru
class TimeoutView(miru.View):
    @miru.button(label="Click me!", style=hikari.ButtonStyle.SUCCESS)
    async def basic_button(self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("You clicked me!")

    async def on_timeout(self) -> None:
        print("This view timed out!")


view = TimeoutView(timeout=10.0)

A risa view in the message has no timeout: it works as long as the message exists. For a lifetime, keep the state in a store with InStore. ttl has no default. Like miru's timeout it counts seconds of inactivity, and every click restarts it.

risa
@risa.register(name="question", state=risa.InStore(ttl=600))
class Question(risa.View):
    text: str

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(self.text),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.yes, label="Yes")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay(f"{self.text} **Yes.**"))

    @classmethod
    async def on_state_missing(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("This question has expired.", ephemeral=True)

The client needs a store for this. A MemoryStore is for trying things out:

client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=risa.MemoryStore())
client.add_view(Question)
Full file 
"""A question that expires, for readers who know miru's timeout."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import hikari

import risa
from risa import ui


@risa.register(name="question", state=risa.InStore(ttl=600))
class Question(risa.View):
    text: str

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(self.text),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.yes, label="Yes")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay(f"{self.text} **Yes.**"))

    @classmethod
    async def on_state_missing(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("This question has expired.", ephemeral=True)


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(
        os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"],
        intents=hikari.Intents.ALL_UNPRIVILEGED | hikari.Intents.MESSAGE_CONTENT,
    )

    client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=risa.MemoryStore())
    client.add_view(Question)

    @bot.listen()
    async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
        if event.content == "!question":
            rendered = await client.build(Question(text="Ship it?"))
            await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

on_timeout() runs when the time is up. risa has no timer, so on_state_missing() runs when someone clicks after the record has expired. Until then the message stays as it is, and risa has no hook for greying out its buttons at that moment.

To end a view yourself, where miru has self.stop(), replace the message with a layout that has no buttons. yes above does that with ctx.edit.

items.title: What risa does not have
items.text:
• Modals. miru has modals, with miru.Modal and ctx.respond_with_modal. risa's are designed but not built, because they wait for hikari to parse Discord's new modal components.
  • Menus and navigators. miru ships miru.ext.menu and miru.ext.nav. In risa you write these yourself, for example as a view with a page: int field.
  • A check before every handler. miru has view_check. In risa, a handler checks ctx.user itself.
  • An error hook. miru has on_error. risa logs what a handler raises, and the click fails for the user unless the handler answered first. Use try in the handler to say something else.
  • Waiting on a view. miru has view.wait() and wait_for_input(). A risa view has no object that lives between clicks, so the code you would run after wait() goes in the handler.
  • Sharing injection with arc. miru has Client.from_arc. risa shares a dependency manager with lightbulb only, through client_from_lightbulb. With arc or crescent, make the client with client_from_app.

items.title: Moving one view at a time
items.text:
A bot can run both, so you need not move everything at once. A risa client answers only the ids risa wrote.

On a gateway bot, make the miru client with ignore_unknown_interactions=True. Without it, miru logs a warning for every click on a risa view.

On a REST bot, hikari has one slot for a component listener, so make the miru client first. risa takes the slot and passes on each click it does not handle, and it logs a warning about that unless you pass warn_shared_listener=False. In the other order, miru's own call to set its listener raises.

items.title: Your first view
items.text: Build a counter: one message with one button, where each click raises the number. It runs on your own bot and keeps counting after a restart.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Install hikari-risa.
  • Create an application in Discord's Developer Portal and copy the token from its Bot page.
  • Invite the bot to a server you can test in, with the scopes bot and applications.commands and the permission to send messages.
  • Put the token in the environment variable DISCORD_TOKEN:
export DISCORD_TOKEN="your-bot-token"

In Windows PowerShell, that is $env:DISCORD_TOKEN = "your-bot-token".

items.title: The view
items.text:
A view is a class. Its fields are its state, render() draws the message from them, and its handlers answer the clicks.

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Part by part:

  • @risa.register(name="counter") tells risa about the class. A click finds its way back to the view by this name, so keep the name once messages are out. Renaming a view retires the buttons already sent.
  • count: int = 0 is the state. risa keeps every annotated field from click to click, and the default is where a new counter starts.
  • render() returns the message's layout, drawn from the fields. ui.Container is a box like an embed, ui.TextDisplay is text in Discord's markdown, and ui.Row holds buttons. risa.ui.nodes lists everything else you can draw.
  • ui.Button(self.click, label="+1") draws a button, and self.click is the handler its clicks go to.
  • @risa.handler makes click a handler. When it runs, the view already holds the state from the click, and ctx is the context of that click.
  • await ctx.rerender() answers the click: it draws the message again from the changed fields and saves them. Discord fails a click that gets no answer within three seconds.

items.title: Send it
items.text:
A view reaches Discord in two steps. Once at startup, you make a client and give it the class with add_view, so that clicks find it. Then, for each message, client.build(Counter()) renders a new view and you send the result.

The two ways below differ in what makes the bot post. Pick one.

lightbulbGateway

/counter posts the counter. Take this one if your bot gets its slash commands from lightbulb. You install it yourself, with uv add hikari-lightbulb or pip install hikari-lightbulb. The metadata of hikari-lightbulb 3.2.6 declares Python below 3.15.

risa_client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client)
risa_client.add_view(Counter)

@lightbulb_client.register()
class CounterCommand(
    lightbulb.SlashCommand,
    name="counter",
    description="Post the counter.",
):
    @lightbulb.invoke
    async def invoke(self, ctx: lightbulb.Context) -> None:
        await ctx.respond(**await risa_client.build(Counter()))

risa.client_from_lightbulb makes a client that shares lightbulb's bot and its dependency manager. build returns a mapping, and ** spreads it into ctx.respond. lightbulb registers /counter with Discord when the bot starts.

Full file 
"""The counter, sent from a lightbulb slash command."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import hikari
import lightbulb

import risa
from risa import ui


@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"])
    lightbulb_client = lightbulb.client_from_app(bot)
    bot.subscribe(hikari.StartingEvent, lightbulb_client.start)

    risa_client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client)
    risa_client.add_view(Counter)

    @lightbulb_client.register()
    class CounterCommand(
        lightbulb.SlashCommand,
        name="counter",
        description="Post the counter.",
    ):
        @lightbulb.invoke
        async def invoke(self, ctx: lightbulb.Context) -> None:
            await ctx.respond(**await risa_client.build(Counter()))

    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Writing !counter in a server channel posts the counter. This is plain hikari, with no other package.

Reading what people write takes a privileged intent. Turn on Message Content Intent on the Bot page of the Developer Portal, or Discord closes the connection when the bot starts.

client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
client.add_view(Counter)

@bot.listen()
async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
    if event.content == "!counter":
        rendered = await client.build(Counter())
        await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

risa.client_from_app makes a client for the bot. send_to sends the built view as a new message, here to the channel the command came from.

items.title: Run it
items.text:
Save the full file of your tab as bot.py and start it:

uv run bot.py

If you installed with pip, that is python bot.py. Post the counter the way your tab does, then click +1. The number in the message goes up.

items.title: Restart it
items.text:
Stop the bot with Ctrl+C, start it again, and click +1 on the same message. The count carries on.

The count is not kept in your bot. When risa draws the button, it writes the count into the button's hidden id, which Discord stores with the message and sends back with every click. On a click, risa reads the count out of the message, rebuilds the view and runs your handler, and ctx.rerender() writes the new count onto the button. A restart loses nothing, and the new process only needs add_view, which your code calls at every start.

A click that lands while the bot is down fails in Discord, which shows that the interaction failed. The count stays where it was, and the next click after the restart works.

The count is not secret.

Anyone who can see the message can read what the button holds, so keep secrets somewhere else.

The message also has limited room: about 60 bytes on one button, and about 70 more for each further one, with the default codec. A view that needs more can move to a store with risa.InStore. Its handlers stay the same, but the move means raising its version, which retires the buttons already sent.

A click changes the id of the button that holds the count, and Discord refuses a click on an id the message no longer has. If two people click at nearly the same moment, the second can fail in Discord and click again. In a store the ids hold a key instead of the count, so clicks leave them as they are, which suits a view many people click at once.

In miru.

A view stops answering after a restart unless you make it persistent. Coming from miru has the whole comparison.

Try it.

Add a button that subtracts one: a second @risa.handler with self.count -= 1, and a second ui.Button in the row. Restart the bot and click +1 on the old message. It keeps its count and gains the new button.

items.title: Installation
items.text: Add hikari-risa to your bot's project. It runs on Python 3.12 to 3.15, and you import it as risa.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uvpip 
uv add hikari-risa

pip install hikari-risa

This also installs what risa depends on: hikari, linkd and msgspec. uv add needs a project to add to, so run uv init first if you have no pyproject.toml yet.

Print the version to check that it worked:

uvpip 
uv run python -c "import risa; print(risa.__version__)"

python -c "import risa; print(risa.__version__)"

items.title: Extras
items.text:
A view keeps its state in its message by default, and that needs nothing extra. Three extras add more:

Extra Installs You want it when redis redis Your views keep their state in Redis, with RedisStore. postgres asyncpg Your views keep their state in PostgreSQL, with PostgresStore. radixly radixly A view runs out of room in its message. The codecs BASE32768 and URO14 fit more than twice as much.

Name one when you install:

uvpip 
uv add "hikari-risa[redis]"

pip install "hikari-risa[redis]"

items.title: Packages your bot may need
items.text:
Two more packages depend on how your bot runs, and hikari-risa installs neither:

  • A bot with slash commands through lightbulb needs hikari-lightbulb.
  • A REST bot needs hikari[server], because hikari's interaction server checks Discord's signatures with it.
